name: Southern Song
info: The second period of the Song dynasty, ruled from Lin'an (now Hangzhou) after the Jin conquest of the north, remembered for its maritime trade, paper money, first permanent navy and Neo-Confucianism.

facts.predecessor: The Northern Song, capital Bianjing (now Kaifeng)

t: After the Jurchen-led Jin dynasty took North China in the Jingkang Incident, the Song court retreated south of the Yangtze and established its capital at Lin'an.
The Song dynasty established China's first permanent navy in 1132, with a headquarters at Dinghai.
Kublai Khan's armies conquered the Southern Song in 1279 after the Battle of Yamen, reuniting China under the Yuan dynasty.
dyk: In 1161, at the Battle of Caishi and the Battle of Tangdao, Song forces of 3,000 men on 120 warships defeated a Jin fleet said to number 70,000 men on 600 warships, using paddle wheel-driven vessels and gunpowder bombs.
ev: The Jurchens capture Kaifeng and the emperors Huizong and Qinzong; Emperor Gaozong withdraws south of the Yangtze
The Song establish China's first permanent navy, with a headquarters at Dinghai
The Song navy defeats the Jin on the Yangtze River in the Battle of Tangdao and the Battle of Caishi
Under Emperor Lizong, Zhu Xi's Four Books and his commentary become standard requirements for the civil service examinations
Möngke Khan dies during the siege of Diaoyu Castle in Chongqing
Kublai blockades the Yangtze River and besieges Xiangyang
Yuan forces capture most of the Song territory, including the capital Lin'an
The Yuan army crushes the last Song resistance in the Battle of Yamen

sections.foundation:
The Song dynasty ruled China from 960. In the 1120s the Song allied with the Jurchen, former subjects of the Liao who had founded the Jin dynasty, and together they conquered the Liao by 1125. Having seen the weakness of the Song army, the Jurchens broke the alliance and began the Jin–Song Wars of 1125 and 1127. The Jin army crossed the North China Plain to Kaifeng, and in the Jingkang Incident it captured the capital, the retired Emperor Huizong, his successor Emperor Qinzong and most of the Imperial court.

The remaining Song forces regrouped under the self-proclaimed Emperor Gaozong (1127–1162), who withdrew south of the Yangtze and established a new capital at Lin'an (modern Hangzhou). This shift of capitals is the dividing line between the Northern and Southern Song. The Jin now held the traditional heartlands around the Yellow River and regarded themselves as the rightful rulers of China, choosing earth, the element that follows the Song's fire, as their dynastic element. Pushed south beyond the Huai River, the Southern Song still held a large population and productive agricultural land, which sustained a robust economy.
sections.socioeconomy:
The Southern Song government sponsored massive shipbuilding and harbour improvement projects, and built beacons and seaport warehouses to support trade abroad through the major international seaports of Quanzhou, Guangzhou and Xiamen. Ships sailed to Korea and Japan, Southeast Asia, the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea. Investors spread their money across many ships, and sea trade spurred an enormous growth in the shipbuilding of Fujian. Many West and Central Asian Muslims came to trade and became a preeminent force in the import and export business.

The Song issued the world's first government paper money, the Jiaozi, and government factories printed it in Huizhou, Chengdu, Hangzhou and Anqi; in 1175 the Hangzhou factory employed more than a thousand workers a day. Hangzhou grew from 200,000 people at the start of the 12th century to 500,000 around 1170, and to over a million a century later. Cities had entertainment quarters, tea houses, theatres and clubs, and festivals such as the Lantern Festival. Peasants owned their own plots, rented as tenants, or were serfs on large estates. Champa rice, introduced in 1011, gave two harvests a year.
sections.military:
To protect its shipping the Southern Song established China's first permanent navy in 1132, with a headquarters at Dinghai. In 1161 the Jin forces under Wanyan Liang (the Prince of Hailing) attacked on the Yangtze River. In the Battle of Tangdao and the Battle of Caishi the Song navy, with swift paddle wheel-driven vessels carrying traction trebuchets that launched gunpowder bombs, won both battles. A century after its founding the navy had 52,000 fighting marines.

The Song military was organized so that the army could not threaten imperial control, often at the expense of effectiveness. The court often believed that successful generals endangered royal authority, and relieved or even executed them, notably Li Gang, Yue Fei and Han Shizhong. Crossbowmen formed their own prized units, and Song soldiers used fire lances, iron-cased bombs and other gunpowder weapons. In the war with the Mongols, the official Li Zengbo wrote in 1259 that Qingzhou was making one to two thousand iron-cased bombshells a month. The Mongols, in turn, employed northern Chinese soldiers and the same gunpowder weapons against the Song, and from 1268 to 1273 Kublai blockaded the Yangtze River with his navy and besieged Xiangyang.
sections.governance:
The emperor ruled through a bureaucracy of scholar-officials. By the Song period the civil service examinations had become virtually the only means of drafting officials, and the number of candidates for the low-level prefectural exams rose from 30,000 a year in the early 11th century to 400,000 by the late 13th century. Only about 20,000 officials were active, so a larger scholarly gentry of candidates, degree-holders, tutors and retired officials took over local affairs, and appointed magistrates relied on their cooperation. Funds for prefectural and county schools came mostly from private financing.

Finance strained the state. To pay for its defences the government confiscated land from the landed gentry, which cost it loyalty among leading families, while wealthy families with connections in office obtained tax-exempt status. The law kept most of the Tang legal code, and the physician and judge Song Ci (1186–1249) wrote a pioneering work of forensic science on examining corpses. Chancellors held great power late in the dynasty: in 1259 Chancellor Jia Sidao ordered the assault that pushed the Mongols back across the Yangtze. In 1241, under Emperor Lizong, Zhu Xi's Four Books and his commentary became required study for the examinations.
sections.impact:
Neo-Confucianism took shape in this age. Zhu Xi (1130–1200), building on the work of Cheng Yi, emphasized the Four Books as an introductory corpus to Confucian learning, and his commentary formed the basis of the Neo-Confucian doctrine. Though his writings were not accepted by his contemporaries, by 1241 they were standard study for the examinations, and Japan and Korea adopted his teaching as Shushigaku and Jujahak. The Chan sect published several major koan collections that remain influential in Zen.

Song merchant shipping carried iron, swords, silk, velvet, porcelain and textiles across the Indian Ocean; the Moroccan geographer al-Idrisi wrote in 1154 of the prowess of Chinese merchant ships there. Gunpowder weapons developed in the Song wars, and by the 14th century the firearm and cannon could be found in Europe, India and the Middle East. Writing flourished too: the poet Li Qingzhao (1084–1151) was famous in her lifetime, and the geographer Fan Chengda (1126–1193) made travel literature popular. Emperor Gaozong commissioned the Eighteen Songs of a Nomad Flute as a diplomatic gesture to the Jin while he negotiated for the release of his mother from captivity.
sections.decline:
The Mongols under Ögedei Khan conquered the Jin dynasty in 1233/34. They had been allied with the Song, but the alliance broke when the Song recaptured the former capitals of Kaifeng, Luoyang and Chang'an. In 1259 Mongol armies attacked in Sichuan, Shandong, Henan and Guangxi, and Möngke Khan died on 11 August during the siege of Diaoyu Castle in Chongqing. Kublai Khan besieged Ezhou, but a coming civil war with his brother Ariq Böke drew him north, and the Song pushed his forces back across the Yangtze. Border skirmishes followed until 1265, when Kublai won a significant battle in Sichuan.

From 1268 to 1273 Kublai besieged Xiangyang, the last obstacle to the Yangtze basin, and in 1271 he declared the Yuan dynasty. In 1275 a Song force of 130,000 troops under Jia Sidao was defeated by the general Bayan, and by 1276 the Yuan held most of the Song territory, including Lin'an. In the Battle of Yamen on the Pearl River Delta in 1279 the Yuan army under Zhang Hongfan crushed the last resistance; the 7-year-old emperor Zhao Bing committed suicide with Prime Minister Lu Xiufu. Emperor Gong was made Duke of Ying and later exiled to Tibet, where he became a monk, and other members of the family, among them the artist Zhao Mengfu, served under the Yuan.

summary: The Southern Song was the Song dynasty after 1127, when the Jin took North China and the court moved to Lin'an. Holding the populous south, it built China's first permanent navy, traded across the Indian Ocean and saw Neo-Confucianism take form, until the Mongols under Kublai Khan conquered it at the Battle of Yamen in 1279.
references: John W. Chaffee, The Cambridge History of China Volume 5 Part Two Sung China, 960-1279 (Cambridge University Press, 2015)
Jacques Gernet, Daily Life in China on the Eve of the Mongol Invasion, 1250–1276 (Stanford University Press, 1962)
F. W. Mote, Imperial China: 900–1800 (Harvard University Press, 1999)
Morris Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times (University of California Press, 1988)

pointDescs.1127: After the Jingkang Incident the Song court regroups under Emperor Gaozong and moves south of the Yangtze to Lin'an.
pointDescs.1132: The Song establish China's first permanent navy, with a headquarters at Dinghai.
pointDescs.1161: The navy defeats the Jin on the Yangtze River at the Battle of Tangdao and the Battle of Caishi.
pointDescs.1170: Hangzhou, the capital, has grown to about 500,000 people from 200,000 at the start of the century.
pointDescs.1234: The Jin dynasty falls to the Mongols, and the Song recapture Kaifeng, Luoyang and Chang'an.
pointDescs.1259: Möngke Khan dies at the siege of Diaoyu Castle, and the Song push Kublai's forces back across the Yangtze.
pointDescs.1265: Kublai wins a significant battle in Sichuan after years of border skirmishes.
pointDescs.1273: Xiangyang falls to Kublai after a siege begun in 1268, opening the Yangtze River basin.
pointDescs.1275: A Song force of 130,000 troops under Jia Sidao is defeated by the general Bayan.
pointDescs.1276: Yuan forces capture most of the Song territory, including the capital Lin'an.
pointDescs.1279: The Yuan army crushes the last Song resistance at the Battle of Yamen, and the boy emperor Zhao Bing dies.

notes: The saved article is the Song dynasty as a whole (960-1279); I kept to what it says of the Southern Song and to dynasty-wide facts it does not limit to the north. Its reference lists are empty, so references are [].
1170 and 1234 point strengths are my judgement; 1273 as the fall of Xiangyang is the end of the siege the article dates 1268 to 1273 (it does not say 'fell').
The Jin fleet figures of 1161 are the article's ('boasted').
